strengths: Timely and practically motivated problem: replacing costly execution-based evaluation of agentic workflows with a learned performance predictor could meaningfully reduce the cost of automated workflow search (e.g., AFlow-style methods).
The proposed multi-view encoding (graph, code, prompt) is a sensible design, and the ablation studies (Tables 4 and 5) reasonably support the contribution of each view and of multi-graph encoding.

Evaluation goes beyond pure prediction accuracy: the paper reports label-ratio experiments demonstrating the value of pretraining in low-label regimes (Figure 3, Figure 4), and a downstream workflow optimization experiment (Table 6) showing the predictor improves selected-workflow quality at zero search cost versus the ground-truth baseline ($39.83).

The paper follows the official FLORA-Bench evaluation protocol and compares against several graph-based baselines (GCN, GAT, GCN-II, Graph Transformer, One For All), reporting means and standard deviations over multiple seeds.
Related work is well organized, including a candid discussion of contemporaneous efforts (FLORA-Bench, MAS-GPT).
weaknesses: Limited novelty over contemporaneous work: FLORA-Bench (Zhang et al., 2025b) already advocates GNN-based predictors of agentic workflow performance; the contribution here is essentially multi-view feature augmentation plus pretraining on top of that idea, and the 'first predictive framework' claim is overstated. Table 1's comparison is somewhat self-serving since MAS-GPT is a workflow generator, not a predictor.

Small and narrow evaluation: only 30-42 workflows per domain and a single benchmark (the AFlow subset of FLORA-Bench). With so few workflows, the random 80/10/10 split over (workflow, task) samples likely places the same workflows in both train and test, raising potential leakage concerns for the accuracy metric; the utility metric partly mitigates this but depends on an unspecified k.

The 'unsupervised pretraining' claim is inconsistent: the contrastive objective requires positive pairs from 'configurations that solve the same task successfully' and negatives from 'failed configurations,' which requires performance labels - contradicting the label-free framing. Details about the pretraining corpus (source, size M, domain composition) are also sparse.

The reconstruction objective is weakly specified: the decoder reconstructs 'input embedding values' of G, C, P rather than the raw structures, so Lrec may amount to reconstructing frozen MiniLM/CodeRankEmbed embeddings, which is close to trivial and its benefit is unclear.

Results are uneven and improvements are moderate: GCN beats the proposed method on reasoning utility (91.82 vs 91.47), the multi-graph ablation lowers code-generation utility (78.52 to 77.22), some ablation rows show suspicious zero variance (e.g., 54.17±0.00), and transferability to HotpotQA is worse than baselines (13.37).

Absolute utility definition and the pass/fail binarization are coarse; the paper itself concedes binary metrics miss nuanced behavior. No statistical significance testing is reported despite modest gaps and three seeds.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code release is mentioned, several methodological details (aggregation layer, CrossGraphAttn configuration, pretraining negatives sampling, k for utility) are underspecified.

Presentation issues: multiple typos ('Math Probelm', 'Codi Generation', 'a workflow-level embeddings') and inconsistencies between improvement numbers quoted in the abstract (12.12%, 15.16%) and main text (9.97%, 6.74%) without clear 'up to' framing in all cases.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: accelerating agentic workflow search via learned performance predictors, analogous to NAS predictors
The framework is clearly described with a well-structured pipeline (multi-view encoding, pretraining, predictor-guided ranking) and a complete algorithm
Ablation studies systematically examine the contribution of each view (code/graph/prompt), multi-graph vs. single-graph encoding, and the effect of pretraining under varying label ratios

Follows the official FLORA-Bench evaluation protocol and reports results over three runs with standard deviations; appendix includes a downstream workflow-optimization experiment and transferability analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method essentially concatenates frozen off-the-shelf embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for prompts, CodeRankEmbed for code) with a standard GNN over workflow graphs, plus generic reconstruction/contrastive pretraining. This is an incremental extension of FLORA-Bench's GNN predictor (Zhang et al., 2025b), with the core 'multi-view' idea amounting to feature concatenation and MLP encoders

The label-scarcity motivation is undermined by methodological inconsistencies: the 'unsupervised' contrastive pretraining defines positive pairs using success labels ('configurations that solve the same task successfully'), so it is not unsupervised; moreover, main experiments train on 80% of samples, which is not a low-label regime

The claimed 'first predictive framework' and the Table 1 comparison against MAS-GPT and FLORA-Bench are qualitative and arguably self-serving; neither close competitor is empirically compared, and the actual baselines (GCN, GAT, GCN-II, Graph Transformer, MLP) are generic and weak. The headroom over the strongest sensible baseline is small (~2% accuracy)

Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (the AFlow subset of FLORA-Bench) with only 30-42 workflows per domain, raising concerns about generalization and statistical strength; accuracy gains are within a few standard deviations in several cells, and the method loses to GCN on reasoning utility

Potential train/test leakage: the random 80/10/10 split is over samples, so the same workflow (and similar tasks) likely appears in both training and test splits, which can inflate accuracy — this is not discussed or controlled for

Downstream optimization results (Table 6) are mixed: HotpotQA performance (13.37%) is substantially worse than GCN/GAT baselines (~19-21%) yet is described as 'broadly comparable', suggesting selective framing
The paper concedes binary pass/fail prediction only, driven by benchmark constraints, which limits the practical utility for cost-aware or multi-objective workflow selection

Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code release, pretraining corpus details are vague, and the theoretical justification for multi-view encoding is asserted as a 'hypothesis' without analysis or evidence beyond aggregate ablations
Writing quality issues (e.g., 'Math Probelm', 'Codi Generation', grammatical errors in the encoder descriptions) and inconsistencies between claimed and reported improvements reduce polish

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and timely: replacing expensive execution-based evaluation of agentic workflow candidates with a learned predictor is a practical direction, and framing it via the NAS performance-predictor literature provides useful context.

The multi-view encoding design (graph, code, prompt views) is sensible and well-motivated by the heterogeneity of agentic workflows; the ablations (Tables 4 and 5) support the claim that all views contribute.

The paper follows the official FLORA-Bench evaluation protocol, reports results over three seeds with standard deviations, and includes ablation studies, label-ratio experiments for the pretraining phase, a downstream workflow-optimization evaluation (Table 6), and a transferability analysis (Appendix A.3).
The end-to-end optimization experiment showing zero search cost versus $39.83 for ground-truth evaluation concretely demonstrates the practical value of the predictor-as-ranker setup.

The paper is clearly written overall, with a precise problem formulation and a complete algorithmic description (Algorithm 1), and it positions itself honestly relative to contemporaneous work (FLORA-Bench, MAS-GPT).
weaknesses: Missing the most important baseline: FLOW-GNN from FLORA-Bench (Zhang et al., 2025b) is the closest existing method and is discussed and differentiated in Section 2 and Table 1, yet it does not appear in the main comparison (Table 3). Without a head-to-head result against FLOW-GNN, the claimed advantage of multi-view over single-view encoding is not directly substantiated empirically.

The absolute gains are modest and possibly within noise: average accuracy improves from 82.67% (GAT) to 84.38% (~1.7 points) and utility from 77.46% to 81.88%, with overlapping standard deviations in several cells. The headline 'up to 12.12%' improvements cherry-pick the single best domain (reasoning), which is a weak basis for the claim of 'substantial improvements'.

The evaluation scale is small: only 30–42 workflows per domain (110 total), so ranking-based utility over roughly 38–42 workflows and exact-match accuracy on a 10% test split are statistically fragile. Three random seeds (2^r) is minimal; no significance testing is provided.

There is a technical inconsistency in the pretraining setup: the contrastive objective requires positive pairs drawn from 'configurations that solve the same task successfully' and negatives including 'failed configurations' — this depends on performance labels, contradicting the claim of 'unsupervised' / 'unlabeled' cross-domain pretraining, which is one of the paper's central contributions.

The technical novelty is moderate: the multi-view encoder is essentially three standard encoders (GNN + two MLPs on frozen MiniLM/CodeRankEmbed embeddings) concatenated through an MLP, and the pretraining objectives (reconstruction + contrastive) are standard; the reconstruction loss is applied to input embeddings rather than raw structures, which further weakens its contribution.

The accuracy metric definition is unclear: if ground-truth performance ē is a continuous success rate, exact-match accuracy 1(ê = ē) is ill-defined without specifying a discretization/binning scheme; this needs clarification for reproducibility.

In the transferability experiment (Appendix A.3), Agentic Predictor is actually worse than GCN and GAT on HotpotQA (13.37% vs. 19.14% and 21.47%), yet this is spun as 'broadly comparable'; the mixed result weakens the generalization claims and deserves more careful treatment.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: no code release is mentioned, and it is unspecified where the unlabeled cross-domain pretraining workflows come from, how they were collected, and how much pretraining data is used — a key cost factor for the method's practicality.

The workflow-optimization study (Appendix A.2) omits the strongest baselines from Table 3 (e.g., Graph Transformer, One For All) and evaluates on only a subset of benchmarks, limiting the strength of the downstream-utility claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: the prohibitive cost of evaluating candidate agentic workflows during automated workflow search, and frames a predictor-based alternative analogous to NAS performance predictors.

The method is clearly presented, with a complete formulation (multi-view encoding across graph/code/prompt views, cross-view attention, contrastive+reconstruction pretraining, lightweight prediction head, predictor-guided search), pseudocode, and an anonymous code repository.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: it follows the official FLORA-Bench protocol, compares against seven graph-based baselines, and includes ablations on input views and multi-graph construction, label-ratio experiments demonstrating the value of pretraining, OOD evaluations (cross-system and cross-domain), robustness across LLM backbones and GNN backbones, comparison with few-shot LLM predictors, a cost/efficiency analysis (Table 6), and downstream workflow-optimization and transferability experiments in the appendix (Tables 13, B.7).

The empirical claims are mostly supported: Agentic Predictor achieves the best average accuracy (79.97%) and utility (76.33%), with consistent gains across most dataset/framework combinations, and the cost analysis provides a concrete break-even argument for predictor-based evaluation over LLM-based scoring.
The paper is transparent about limitations (binary success metrics only, single-benchmark dependence) and includes a reproducibility statement with fixed random seeds and an LLM-usage disclosure.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental relative to the closest prior work. FLORA-Bench (Zhang et al., 2025c) already proposes GNN-based predictors for agentic workflow performance on the same benchmark; the main deltas here (extra code/prompt views as MLP-encoded global features, standard contrastive/reconstruction pretraining) are relatively conventional multi-view/self-supervised techniques re-applied, and Table 1's claimed distinctions are somewhat superficial (e.g., code and prompt encoders are simple L-layer MLPs over frozen embeddings).

Headline improvements are modest and partially overstated. Average accuracy improvement is +1.61% over the best baseline, with per-domain deltas as small as +0.09% (CodeGD) and even a negative delta for utility on ReasonAF (-0.35%), yet the abstract/intro advertise 'up to 6.90%'/'up to 5.87%'. The best-baseline improvements are near the reported standard deviations on several cells, and no statistical significance testing is provided despite only three seeds.

Evaluation is confined to a single third-party benchmark (FLORA-Bench), which the authors themselves constructed their method around; 'carefully curated' in the abstract oversells what is in fact a reuse of an existing benchmark. Label construction (how ground-truth success/fail labels are derived, number of execution samples per label) is not clearly described, and exact-match 'accuracy' on estimated success labels may be a noisy metric.

The 'cross-domain' pretraining claim is weakened by the pretraining corpus composition: M=232,104 unlabeled workflows are 90.58% from the Reasoning domain, drawn only from training splits of the same benchmark, so the pretraining is neither well balanced across domains nor truly cross-corpus. The cost of this pretraining (168s/epoch, 13.5GB) is non-trivial relative to baselines.

The integration with workflow optimization is treated as secondary: the actual search instantiation is simply random sampling plus predictor re-ranking, and the main optimization results are relegated to the appendix; the framing as 'search-agnostic' partly avoids engaging with whether the predictor helps in realistic iterative search loops (e.g., active learning or predictor-in-the-loop refinement).

Some results are internally puzzling and under-discussed, e.g., in the ablation (Table 4) the Graph+Text configuration collapses to 54.17% accuracy on reasoning, and the Mistral 7B backbone case (Table 7) where Agentic Predictor is not the best model is only briefly acknowledged.

strengths: The problem of label-efficient performance prediction for agentic workflows is timely and practically relevant; reducing expensive LLM-based candidate evaluation in workflow search is a meaningful goal.

The paper is built on a concrete, well-motivated framework (multi-view graph/code/prompt encoding plus optional self-supervised pretraining) and is clearly written and well-organized, with good positioning against FLORA-Bench, MAS-GPT, and NAS predictors.

The empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive for the benchmark used: main comparisons against 7 baselines across 3 domains and 2 frameworks, ablations on views and graph multiplicity, label-ratio experiments with pretraining, OOD (cross-system and cross-domain) tests, LLM-based predictor baselines, backbone robustness, cost analysis, and a downstream workflow-optimization experiment.

The cost/efficiency analysis (break-even point vs. LLM scoring, amortization of training cost) is a useful practical contribution, and the zero-search-cost workflow optimization results (Table 13) provide evidence of end-to-end utility beyond raw prediction accuracy.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core ideas — multi-view/multi-graph encoding of workflow configurations, self-supervised pretraining of encoders, and predictor-as-ranker guided search — are standard techniques transplanted from NAS (BRP-NAS, CAP, FlowerFormer, CATE) and multimodal learning. The delta over FLORA-Bench (which already proposes GNN predictors on this exact benchmark) is essentially feature enrichment plus a pretraining stage, and the paper does not identify a fundamentally new insight about what makes workflow performance predictable.

Marginal and mixed empirical gains. Average accuracy improvements over the best baseline are small (+1.61% absolute, with per-dataset deltas as low as +0.09% on CodeGD and even -0.35% utility on ReasonAF). Given three random seeds and no statistical significance testing, many of these differences may not be meaningful, yet the abstract claims improvements 'up to 6.90%' — a cherry-picked figure from the most favorable cell.

Potential evaluation leakage. With tens of thousands of samples generated from only 38-30 workflow configurations per framework (Table 2), a random 80/10/10 split over instances means the same (or near-identical) workflow appears in train and test. Models can largely memorize workflow-level success rates rather than generalizing; the reported 'accuracy' may substantially overstate true predictive ability, and the paper never evaluates the more honest split (held-out workflows).

Several technical components are unclear or questionable: (i) the contrastive objective is described confusingly — positives are cross-view embeddings of the same configuration while negatives are other configurations in the batch, making the loss as written atypical; (ii) the graph branch 'reconstructs its own embedding with a stop-gradient,' which makes the reconstruction target circular and its benefit unclear; (iii) the decoder reconstructs 'input embeddings' rather than actual graphs/code/prompts, weakening the reconstruction claim.

The 'cross-domain' pretraining corpus is drawn from the same benchmark's training splits and is heavily skewed (90.58% reasoning samples), so the claimed cross-domain transferability is weakly supported; no experiment isolates pretraining gains on a genuinely disjoint external domain.

The search instantiation is minimal — predictor-guided random sampling of K candidates — and the main evaluation focuses on prediction metrics; the actual search acceleration story (the paper's central motivation) is only briefly supported in §B.6 rather than being a first-class experiment.

Single-benchmark dependency: all experiments use FLORA-Bench with binary pass/fail labels, which the authors themselves acknowledge in limitations; this narrows the scope and significance of the conclusions.

Reproducibility statement contains an empty/blank repository link in the text as presented, and there are presentation errors (e.g., 'few-show', formatting glitches in Table 6), suggesting insufficient polish.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: accelerating candidate evaluation in automated agentic workflow search via learned performance predictors is a timely and practically relevant direction, and the paper positions itself well relative to NAS performance predictors and recent agentic-workflow search systems (AFlow, G-Designer, MAS-GPT, FLORA-Bench).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper covers main comparisons against seven strong baselines across six dataset-framework combinations, ablations on views and graph encodings, GNN-backbone and LLM-backbone robustness checks, low-label pretraining experiments, OOD (cross-system and cross-domain) generalization, LLM-based few-shot predictor comparison, downstream workflow-optimization results, and resource/cost analysis.

The predictor-guided search experiment (Table 13) is a valuable addition: it demonstrates the predictor actually helps downstream workflow optimization (74.43% vs. 68-71% for GNN predictors and 62.56% random) at near-zero search cost, which supports the practical claim beyond prediction accuracy alone.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: pseudocode, implementation details (encoders, truncation lengths, hyperparameters), seeds, and an anonymous code repository are provided; resource usage and inference cost are quantified.
The paper is honest about limitations (binary success metric only, single benchmark dependence) and follows the benchmark's official evaluation protocol for fair comparison.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea—training a predictor on richer representations of candidate configurations—closely follows established NAS predictor literature, and the contribution over the very recent FLORA-Bench (Zhang et al., 2025c) is essentially 'use multi-view features (code/prompt embeddings) plus self-supervised pretraining instead of a single-view GNN'. The technical components (GNN, MLP encoders, cross-view attention, contrastive + reconstruction losses, task-embedding concatenation) are all standard; there is little methodological depth or analysis of why multi-view fusion works.

Evidence for some central claims is thin. Gains are sometimes marginal or inconsistent: e.g., CodeGD accuracy improvement is +0.09% (within noise), and Agentic Predictor actually loses to GCN on ReasonAF utility (-0.35%). Given only 3 seeds and standard deviations of similar magnitude, several headline improvements may not be statistically significant; no significance testing is reported.

The pretraining corpus is severely imbalanced (90.58% Reasoning, 6.56% Code, 2.86% Math), yet the paper claims 'cross-domain' pretraining benefits. The effect of this skew is not analyzed, and the pretraining experiment does not disentangle whether gains come from cross-domain transfer or simply more unlabeled in-domain data.

The method section has clarity issues: the reconstruction objective is described ambiguously (the graph branch 'reconstructs its own embedding target' while code/prompt are 'reconstructed in input space'—what exactly the decoder targets and how L_rec on graphs is computed given G_hat = MLP(Z_G) is unclear); the contrastive loss formula is informal; and Table 1's comparison is self-serving without empirical ablation against FLORA-Bench's own predictor configuration with added features.

Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (FLORA-Bench), whose workflows come from only two frameworks (G-Designer, AFlow) with similar average node counts (~6), limiting evidence for generality claims about 'heterogeneous agentic workflows'. The binary pass/fail formulation also discards score information, acknowledged but not addressed.

Some experiments lack detail or raise questions: Table 9 accuracy (84.97%) differs from the main results (79.97%) without explanation of the differing protocol; the anonymous repository link appears blank in the PDF; and the 'search-agnostic' positioning is not really exercised—the search integration is limited to random sampling + ranking.
